newsitem.title: UK: MPs criticise Bank of England over Barings.
newsitem.headline: MPs criticise Bank of England over Barings.

text.p: The Bank of England might need to be stripped of its responsibility for supervising Britain's banks unless it learns the lessons of last year's collapse of Barings, a powerful parliamentary committee said on Tuesday.

The House of Commons Treasury Select Committee expressed concern that the central bank, as a former bank itself and a "cheerleader" for the City, might shy away from measures that would displease the banks or impair London's competitiveness.

"The Bank needs to demonstrate that it is able to separate its supervisory activities from its other functions and avoid any possible weakening of its regulatory effectiveness due to its proximity to the day-to-day banking market.
"Otherwise it may be that in order to bring about the necessary cultural change banking supervision will have to be taken away from the Bank of England," the panel said.

Barings, Britain's oldest merchant bank, collapsed early in 1995 under the weight of more than $1 billion in speculative losses chalked up by Singapore-based trader Nick Leeson, who is now serving a jail sentence in the south-east Asian city state.

A report by Britain's Board of Banking Supervision in July 1995 identified a number of lessons arising from the affair and made 17 recommendations for the Bank of England (BoE), which accepted them in full.

The Treasury committee welcomed the extra resources that the BoE is pumping into supervision to keep closer tabs on banks as they expand into risky securities markets. Barings collapsed because Leeson made a huge, unauthorised gamble in futures and options contracts that went horribly wrong.
But the cross-party panel of members of parliament expressed concern that, despite recent changes at senior level in the central bank, its "old culture" will persist.
"The Bank has tried in the past to assure us that a new era has commenced in its supervisory wing and so we are concerned that this may be another false dawn," the report said.

The MPs said the Barings case illustrated "considerable weaknesses" and "obvious shortcomings" in the BoE's supervisory regime in areas such as the evaluation of internal controls at banks, internal communication at the central bank itself, and the application of its existing rules.
It said the bank's proximity to the banking sector was a double-edged sword.

"While it is useful to the Bank to have intimate knowledge of the banking sector (although not intimate enough to have picked up on the rumours circulating before the collapse of Barings) there is a risk that the Bank could avoid introducing useful supervisory measures which would displease the banks or might be perceived to have competitive implications," it said.
In a brief reaction, a spokesman for the Bank of England said: "The report identifies some of the dilemmas that face regulators and we welcome it as a constructive contribution to the debate.".
